segment: operations, ownership, security, wallet custody, integrations, and node operations
scope: Official BTCPay Server documentation branches inspected for server ownership and account/store roles, account security, wallet custody and signing, integrations/API/webhooks/plugins, deployment and maintenance, backup/restore, multistore, mobile availability, on-chain node operation, and Lightning connection/liquidity/backup. Findings describe documented behaviors and conditions, not tested compatibility. Merchant-facing POS, invoice/payment-request, refund, payout, and reporting workflows are assigned to another researcher. This is a bounded corpus, not an exhaustive product inventory.

claims.capability: A user can enable two-factor authentication on their account and save recovery codes.
claims.merchant_outcome: A merchant can add a second authentication factor and retain recovery access if the factor is lost.
claims.trigger: Account setup or settings visit
claims.behavior: User Guide tells users to enable account 2FA and store recovery codes safely.
preconditions: User can access the account settings
The instance permits the configured authentication method
qualifiers: Exact factors and account policy may vary by version/instance
recovery_edge_cases: Lost factor can require administrator recovery; docs advise preserving recovery codes
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Offer a guided account-security checklist that tracks completion without storing recovery codes.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Account takeover can expose store operations and any server-held hot-wallet keys; the value is relevant to Bitcoin merchants regardless of payment rails.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Extra login friction and recovery-code custody burden; avoid implying 2FA protects a separately held seed from server/operator compromise.
claims.acceptance_test: For an account with 2FA available, setup guidance leads the user to enable it and confirm recovery codes are stored, without collecting their secret values.

claims.capability: A server administrator can control open registration and require email confirmation under server policies.
claims.merchant_outcome: An operator can restrict account creation to approved users or require email confirmation when allowing registration.
claims.trigger: Server Settings > Policies configuration
claims.behavior: Policy settings allow registration and can require email confirmation when SMTP is configured.
preconditions: Administrator access
Email confirmation requires working SMTP
qualifiers: Instance policy applies across users; registration can be disabled
recovery_edge_cases: Admin can instead invite selected users; invitations depend on configured email for email delivery
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Present registration state, confirmation requirement, and invite route together in an operator setup status view.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: This is general account governance and does not depend on Bitcoin settlement or custody.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Closed registration improves access control but creates operator work to onboard staff; open registration can increase spam exposure.
claims.acceptance_test: Admin can see current registration/confirmation settings and invite route, and a test registration behaves according to the selected policies.

claims.capability: A user can create additional stores from the store selector, each with its own business/project identity and settings.
claims.merchant_outcome: A merchant can separate business or project payment configuration into distinct stores.
claims.trigger: Choose Create Store in store selector
claims.behavior: BTCPay prompts for store name and default pricing currency; store settings may later be changed.
preconditions: User account exists and policy permits store creation
qualifiers: Store quota or admin policy may limit availability
recovery_edge_cases: New store does not receive on-chain payments until a wallet is configured
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Prompt to configure wallet ownership and access roles before presenting a new store as ready to receive funds.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Separate stores can isolate settings and accounting contexts while preserving direct control over configured receiving wallets.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: More stores create configuration and staff-access overhead; store separation alone does not establish separate keys or legal entities.
claims.acceptance_test: Creating a second store produces an independent store context and clearly shows its wallet setup prerequisite before indicating on-chain readiness.

claims.capability: A store owner can invite/add store users and assign predefined store roles including Owner, Manager, Employee, or Guest.
claims.merchant_outcome: A merchant can provide coworkers access at the store level using role assignments.
claims.actor: store user with store settings permission
claims.trigger: Adding or inviting a user to the store
claims.behavior: The default flow creates an invitation; direct add without invitation requires server-settings permission; role can be changed later.
preconditions: Store settings permission
Target account/email exists or can accept invitation
qualifiers: Exact effective permissions should be checked against target instance roles/version
recovery_edge_cases: Removing the last Owner is rejected; invitations can be cancelled or resent
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Show a plain-language, permission-difference preview before inviting staff or changing a role.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Store-scoped roles can reduce how many staff can alter payment settings or wallet operations, useful in key-sensitive Bitcoin commerce.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: More role administration; role labels alone do not prove granular segregation across all plugin-contributed permissions.
claims.acceptance_test: Invite flow identifies role scope and permission summary; removing the sole store owner is prevented with a recovery path.

claims.capability: Server settings are restricted to server administrators, distinct from a user's store-level authority.
claims.merchant_outcome: An operator can govern instance-wide policies and maintenance separately from ordinary store operations.
claims.trigger: Opening server settings or performing server-wide operations
claims.behavior: Server Settings documentation identifies its settings as server-admin only; API defines separate server and store permission scopes.
preconditions: User has an administrator/server permission
qualifiers: Specific API operations and permissions vary with version and plugins
recovery_edge_cases: Newly promoted server admin may not automatically be a member of existing stores in version 2.0+
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Make the server-admin versus store-owner boundary visible on every permission management screen.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Separating infrastructure administration from store access can limit who changes server node and key-related configuration.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Operations may depend on a small number of admins; ensure ownership succession and access recovery.
claims.acceptance_test: A store-only user cannot open or mutate server settings, and promoted admins are prompted to join needed stores.

claims.capability: A merchant can connect an existing supported wallet by importing public wallet data while keeping its private keys off the server.
claims.merchant_outcome: Store can derive receiving data for an existing wallet without handing BTCPay the spending key.
claims.trigger: Select connect existing wallet and provide supported public wallet information
claims.behavior: The user guide describes importing public wallet data from supported hardware/software wallets and says this keeps private keys off the server.
preconditions: Supported wallet data and compatible derivation configuration
qualifiers: A third-party host can still redirect future receiving addresses if malicious; documentation recommends independent wallet monitoring
recovery_edge_cases: Never enter an existing seed into an internet-connected server; use extended public information
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Explain what public wallet data reveals and provide a receiving-address verification step on a trusted wallet.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Merchant retains signing authority and can validate derived addresses independently, fitting Bitcoin self-custody practice.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Public derivation data can expose wallet activity/privacy; a compromised or malicious host may substitute future receive destinations.
claims.acceptance_test: Setup imports no private key, displays a test receive address that matches an independent wallet derivation, and flags mismatch.

claims.capability: A merchant may generate wallet receiving data on the server and erase the private key from it, leaving spend authorization to an external signer or recovery seed.
claims.merchant_outcome: Server can display wallet activity and receive funds without retaining the generated wallet's spending key after watch-only setup.
claims.trigger: Create a new watch-only wallet
claims.behavior: The guide states the private key is erased from server and spending requires recovery seed or external signer.
preconditions: User can generate a wallet; host policy may disable generation for non-admins
qualifiers: Recovery seed is still a bearer secret and must be recorded offline
recovery_edge_cases: Test recovery and signing before accepting significant value
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Make the seed backup and successful recovery proof mandatory readiness steps before enabling high-value receipt.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Separates server availability from spending control if seed custody remains with the merchant.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Seed loss can make funds unspendable; seed theft enables spending; receiving service still depends on server availability.
claims.acceptance_test: After watch-only setup, server can show receive address but cannot sign a spend; recovered external signer can sign a small test transaction.

claims.capability: A merchant can create a hot wallet whose private key is held on the server and use BTCPay interface signing.
claims.merchant_outcome: The merchant can spend through BTCPay without an external signer workflow.
claims.trigger: Choose create hot wallet and enable server signing
claims.behavior: The guide identifies server-held key, interface spending convenience, and increased exposure if account or server is compromised.
preconditions: Server policy permits hot wallet creation
qualifiers: Appropriate only for balances aligned with server and account security
recovery_edge_cases: Keep seed/recovery material offline and test recovery
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Add balance exposure limits and an explicit custody disclosure at hot-wallet creation.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Immediate in-interface control can serve small operational balances while settlement remains Bitcoin-native.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Server/account compromise can expose funds; user convenience concentrates signing authority in online infrastructure.
claims.acceptance_test: Setup plainly identifies that private key will remain on server and requires confirmation; test spend works and key recovery instructions are available.

claims.capability: The internal wallet displays on-chain incoming, outgoing, and unconfirmed transactions with timestamps, balances, labels, and transaction details.
claims.merchant_outcome: Merchant can inspect its server-observed on-chain wallet activity and open transaction details.
claims.trigger: Open Wallets for a configured store wallet
claims.behavior: Transactions are sorted by date; statuses use incoming/outgoing/unconfirmed distinctions and transaction IDs open details/explorer links.
preconditions: Store wallet configured and chain data available
qualifiers: Internal BTCPay wallet shows on-chain payments only; Lightning funds are managed separately
recovery_edge_cases: Sync lag can delay visibility; independently verify expected funds
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Show data freshness and node sync status beside wallet balance and distinguish pending from confirmed funds.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Merchant can audit Bitcoin transactions against its own full-node-backed wallet view without a custodial payment processor ledger.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Node synchronization and chain reorgs affect observed status; user must not confuse unconfirmed with final settlement.
claims.acceptance_test: Known confirmed, unconfirmed, incoming and outgoing test transactions render with consistent status, timestamps and transaction IDs.

claims.capability: BTCPay can construct a PSBT for spending; a compatible external wallet signs it and the signed PSBT is returned to BTCPay for finalization and broadcast.
claims.merchant_outcome: Merchant can authorize a spend without placing the signing key on BTCPay server.
claims.trigger: Create send and select compatible PSBT/hardware signing route
claims.behavior: Workflow constructs unsigned inputs/outputs, exports PSBT, external wallet inspects/signs, imports signed PSBT, BTCPay forms transaction and user verifies/broadcasts.
preconditions: Configured wallet derivation path and compatible PSBT signer
User can independently inspect transaction
qualifiers: Hardware support is Bitcoin only; signing software/device compatibility varies
recovery_edge_cases: Incorrect AccountKeyPath can prevent spend; verify final transaction before broadcast
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Make fee, destination, change, and signer compatibility verification explicit in a staged review screen.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: External key control plus PSBT inspection aligns with Bitcoin's open signing tools and avoids a hosted custodian for the spend.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Adds export/import steps and depends on correct derivation metadata and hardware compatibility.
claims.acceptance_test: A test PSBT round trip preserves intended inputs, destination, amount, change and fee; device signature finalizes and broadcast is independently visible.

claims.capability: Greenfield is the documented primary REST API for new integrations and provides endpoints across server/store operations, with plugin-contributed endpoints possible.
claims.merchant_outcome: A developer can automate documented BTCPay operations or integrate an external commerce backend.
claims.trigger: Plan integration against a BTCPay instance
claims.behavior: Docs recommend Greenfield for new work; instance /docs and OpenAPI show its deployed version and installed-plugin API surface; legacy BitPay API remains for compatibility with no guarantee of current BitPay compatibility.
preconditions: Instance URL and relevant store ID
Deployed API offers needed operation
qualifiers: Documentation of endpoint is not proof of compatibility with every instance
recovery_edge_cases: If endpoint differs, inspect target instance /docs and plugin set
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Provide an instance compatibility preflight that compares required operations and permissions before integration setup.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: A documented open API can connect Bitcoin-native settlement to diverse merchant systems without requiring payment processor custody.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Integrators bear compatibility and operational maintenance across self-hosted versions/plugins; API access is not itself a Bitcoin-specific benefit.
claims.acceptance_test: Integration preflight discovers the target instance's API schema and confirms each required operation and permission before creating a live invoice.

claims.capability: API keys can be restricted by permissions and stores; interactive authorization lets a third-party integration ask the user for selected access without sharing their password.
claims.merchant_outcome: Merchant can connect an app with a bounded set of capabilities and revoke/reconnect its credentials.
claims.trigger: App authorization or API-key creation
claims.behavior: Docs recommend interactive authorization for third-party apps; keys should be scoped to needed stores/least privilege, kept server-side, encrypted and revocable; manual keys are available for prototyping.
preconditions: User can authorize application and selected permission/store set exists
qualifiers: Basic auth is unusually broad and limited to initial account window or explicitly enabled; exact instance policies vary
recovery_edge_cases: If key is exposed or permission scope must change, revoke and reconnect; writes need app-side idempotency
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Show a human-readable permission rationale and accessible revoke control for every connected app.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Least privilege limits third-party software's ability to modify store settings or initiate operations around Bitcoin funds.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Narrow scope may break app functions; broad permissions or client-side secrets undermine the security benefit.
claims.acceptance_test: Authorization names store and each permission, omits password disclosure, and successfully rejects an out-of-scope operation.

claims.capability: BTCPay signs webhook payloads with a per-webhook secret and receiving integration can verify the HMAC signature over the raw request body.
claims.merchant_outcome: Backend can reject forged or altered callbacks before taking action on a payment event.
claims.trigger: Webhook delivery arrives at configured endpoint
claims.behavior: Docs specify BTCPay-Sig HMAC-SHA256 verification using webhook secret and recommend preserving raw body before parsing.
preconditions: Webhook secret provisioned securely and exact body retained
qualifiers: Webhook notifications are distinct from legacy BitPay notification/IPN format
recovery_edge_cases: Bad signature must not advance order; reconcile through authenticated API if event delivery is missed
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Ship test vectors and an integration health check that validates raw-body signature handling.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Authenticating callbacks prevents false fulfillment when a backend uses Bitcoin payment state to release goods.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Signature verification authenticates source, not final settlement or truth of a stale event; API reconciliation remains necessary.
claims.acceptance_test: Valid signed event is accepted; changed body or wrong secret is rejected; duplicate delivery is handled idempotently.

claims.capability: Store webhooks can be configured for chosen event types and automatic redelivery of failed deliveries.
claims.merchant_outcome: Merchant's integration can recover from temporary receiver failures without manual resending for each delivery.
claims.trigger: Create or edit store webhook and enable automatic redelivery
claims.behavior: Docs describe retry attempts after 10 seconds, one minute, then up to six attempts after 10 minutes; delivery IDs indicate redelivery.
preconditions: Reachable payload URL and configured secret; webhook enabled
qualifiers: Retry is finite and does not guarantee successful fulfillment
Events are store-scoped
recovery_edge_cases: Backend should process duplicates safely and reconcile missed events by GET API
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Expose delivery history and a reconciliation action in webhook settings.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Reliable callback delivery is settlement-rail agnostic, though Bitcoin merchant fulfillment depends on it.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Retries can create duplicate work if consumer is not idempotent; finite retries still require reconciliation.
claims.acceptance_test: Simulated endpoint outage triggers the documented retry sequence; duplicate deliveries do not create duplicate fulfillment.

claims.capability: Plugins run inside the BTCPay Server process and may access server services and data.
claims.merchant_outcome: An administrator can extend the instance but must evaluate plugins as code with a broad server trust boundary.
claims.trigger: Install plugin from directory or other source
claims.behavior: Docs warn plugin listing is not a security audit or endorsement and recommend reviewing source, maintainer and compatibility, and keeping backups.
preconditions: Administrator can manage plugins and source/version is available for review
qualifiers: Plugin author, code, release and support vary
recovery_edge_cases: Uninstall is scheduled and only applies after server restart, causing temporary unavailability
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Present plugin permissions, code provenance, version compatibility, and backup state before install.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Plugins can add useful Bitcoin workflows while broad runtime access creates material risk to store data and operational infrastructure.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Plugin extensibility increases capability and ecosystem choice but expands supply-chain and availability risk.
claims.acceptance_test: Install screen discloses runtime access and source/version; uninstall status remains visible until restart completes.

claims.capability: Removing an installed plugin schedules removal that takes effect after BTCPay server restart.
claims.merchant_outcome: Operator can remove a plugin from active installation after a planned restart.
claims.trigger: Uninstall plugin and restart server
claims.behavior: Plugin documentation says uninstall is scheduled and removal takes effect after restart; service is temporarily unavailable during restart.
preconditions: Plugin installed and administrator can restart instance
qualifiers: Restart affects instance availability
recovery_edge_cases: Verify plugin no longer appears after server returns
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Show scheduled state and maintenance window impact before restart.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Restart lifecycle is general software operations, independent of Bitcoin settlement.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Restart interrupts checkout and management access; deferring it leaves plugin active longer.
claims.acceptance_test: After restart the plugin is absent from installed list and core store/wallet functions remain available.

claims.capability: Docker backup script archives database dumps, generated secrets and Docker volumes, with optional archive encryption, and restarts the BTCPay stack afterward.
claims.merchant_outcome: Operator can create a restorable instance data archive while excluding re-downloadable blockchain data and caches.
claims.trigger: Run btcpay-backup.sh
claims.behavior: Script dumps databases, stops stack, archives selected data, optionally encrypts, restarts stack, and cleans temporary dumps.
preconditions: Docker deployment; script run as root; enough local storage
qualifiers: Backup scripts have deployment limits; docs say restore-test before reliance
Backup validation/compression occur while stack is stopped
recovery_edge_cases: Backup is not a complete deployment profile; preserve environment/deployment settings separately
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Provide a guided backup job with off-host copy, retention, and restore-test status.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Merchant can retain its own payment records and wallet metadata without relying on a payment processor's custodial database.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Backup downtime, encryption passphrase custody and operator responsibility add burden; archive does not preserve blockchain data or prove funds can be recovered.
claims.acceptance_test: Restore a recent encrypted and unencrypted sample into isolated compatible deployment and compare stores, records, wallet metadata and service readiness.

claims.capability: Operator must separately arrange protected off-host storage and retention; default backup script replaces the local archive and does not provide retention or remote copy.
claims.merchant_outcome: A merchant can avoid treating one local archive as a resilient backup by creating a separate copy/retention process.
claims.trigger: Configure backup strategy
claims.behavior: Documentation says each default run replaces the same local archive, script provides neither retention nor off-host copy, and cron failures should be monitored.
preconditions: Operator controls external protected storage and monitoring
qualifiers: Specific copy/retention system not prescribed
recovery_edge_cases: Silent cron failures or local disk loss can remove the only usable backup
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Include optional built-in encrypted offsite copies, rotation policy, and restore drill reminders.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: A recoverable local node/store operation supports merchant independence from third-party processors.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Offsite encryption expands key custody obligations and recurring storage cost; backups must be tested rather than assumed.
claims.acceptance_test: A scheduled backup creates versioned protected remote copies, reports failures, and a selected retained copy restores in isolation.

claims.capability: Restore validates archive mode and Bitcoin LND destination conditions, restores volumes/database/secrets and has safeguards against overlaying existing LND data.
claims.merchant_outcome: Operator can restore instance data while reducing the risk of mixing restored wallet/channel state with unrelated destination data.
claims.trigger: Run btcpay-restore.sh with archive
claims.behavior: Restore checks archive mode/data, stops stack, preserves backed-up SCB separately when applicable, imports databases, then starts default restore or leaves migration restore stopped.
preconditions: Compatible deployment profile, generated Compose file and required BTCPay volume prepared
Correct script/archive type and passphrase if encrypted
qualifiers: Restore success is not proof of application health, HTTPS, chain synchronization or Lightning recovery
recovery_edge_cases: Errors after shutdown may leave stack stopped; inspect services and use isolated restore for Lightning data
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Turn restore into a preflight/recovery checklist showing archive mode, config compatibility, LND data presence and post-restore verification steps.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Recovery of a self-run payment stack can preserve merchant operational data and on-chain wallet monitoring under merchant control.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Incorrect stale channel state can risk funds; restore requires operator skill and does not validate external network readiness.
claims.acceptance_test: Restore refuses wrong-mode or nonempty-LND overlays, then isolated recovery verifies store data and on-chain sync without connecting stale Lightning state to peers.

claims.capability: For Bitcoin LND using default bbolt, a default backup may preserve wallet and static channel backup but omits channel database; recovery requires manual SCB verification/import and requests peer force closes.
claims.merchant_outcome: Operator can recover eligible channel funds after default restore, understanding it does not recreate open channels or guarantee recovery.
claims.trigger: Default restore of Bitcoin LND data then execute printed recovery commands
claims.behavior: Docs distinguish SCB recovery from planned migration; preserve SCB, verify it, import it only into original wallet/network, monitor pending channels and wallet balance.
preconditions: Correct LND seed/wallet and usable SCB
Peers respond; on-chain fees available
qualifiers: Does not recover every in-flight HTLC or cover channels opened after SCB; no fixed recovery time
Not generalized to other LN implementations
recovery_edge_cases: Do not import SCB after successful migration; stale channel databases or running both nodes can cause loss
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Expose implementation-specific recovery mode and separate SCB freshness tracking before shutdown or restore.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Self-custodial Lightning can remain merchant-controlled, but protocol recovery constraints put operational burden and counterparty dependency on merchant.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: SCB disaster recovery force-closes channels, incurs fees and depends on peer availability; backup freshness matters for recovery materials.
claims.acceptance_test: In isolated recovery drill, verify seed/SCB identity and signature, import SCB, observe pending force-closes and reconcile recovered balance without starting original node.

claims.capability: A Docker operator can create a migration-mode backup that includes Bitcoin LND channel graph data, leaves source stack stopped and restores to a compatible prepared destination in stopped state.
claims.merchant_outcome: A merchant can move a healthy LND node while preserving current open-channel database state if source remains stopped and migration snapshot is current.
claims.trigger: Run btcpay-backup.sh --migrate then btcpay-restore.sh --migrate on destination
claims.behavior: Migration archives channel graph and other LND data while excluding blockchain data; destination restore remains stopped until explicit review/start.
preconditions: Compatible destination deployment and LND version
Disable source scheduled backups, updates, restart jobs; source data remains unchanged after snapshot
qualifiers: Specific workflow is Bitcoin LND; migration archive does not make an outdated snapshot safe
recovery_edge_cases: Never run original and restored nodes simultaneously; if source changed after snapshot, take new migration backup
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Offer a guarded migration workflow with source freeze verification and destination readiness comparison.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Allows a merchant to operate and migrate its self-custodial Lightning node rather than moving funds into a hosted custodian.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Migration has a strict single-active-node invariant and requires correct channel state, compatible deployment and sufficient operator expertise.
claims.acceptance_test: Migration drill confirms source stopped and unchanged, destination restored stopped, channel state matches, and exactly one node is started.

claims.capability: Docker operator can update through UI maintenance or shell; update pulls the checked-out branch, regenerates stack configuration and recreates services.
claims.merchant_outcome: Operator can apply software and service configuration updates through documented maintenance routes.
claims.trigger: Click Update in server maintenance or run btcpay-update.sh
claims.behavior: Update pulls branch, ensures Docker versions, archives retrievable Compose logs, regenerates compose/routes/secrets, rewrites wrappers/environment and recreates stack.
preconditions: Docker deployment and usable operator access/profile
qualifiers: Significant upgrades should be preceded by backup and release-note review
Generated Compose manual edits are overwritten
recovery_edge_cases: Update may cause temporary service interruption; inspect pre-update logs if issue follows
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Show backup freshness, release notes, expected downtime and rollback evidence in update workflow.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Update mechanics apply across payment products; Bitcoin merchants must additionally protect node/wallet state during changes.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Updates can fix bugs but service recreation interrupts payment acceptance; regeneration can remove manual customizations.
claims.acceptance_test: A staged update records prior logs, recreates services, preserves configured stores/wallets and reports chain/node readiness before resuming acceptance.

claims.capability: Docker update cleanup defaults to removing unused Docker images across the host, including unrelated images, except generator-labeled images.
claims.merchant_outcome: Operator can reclaim image storage after updates but must account for shared-host workloads.
claims.trigger: Update completes with BTCPAY_UPDATE_CLEAN=true default
claims.behavior: Cleanup removes unused images beyond BTCPay-specific images unless configured otherwise.
preconditions: Operator host uses Docker and default cleanup remains enabled
qualifiers: Host-level side effects reach unrelated images
recovery_edge_cases: Unrelated services may need to re-pull removed images before restart
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Scope cleanup to BTCPay-owned images by default and offer host-wide cleanup as a separately explicit action.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: This behavior does not depend on Bitcoin; it affects host operations supporting a Bitcoin service.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Broad cleanup can reclaim disk but disrupt unrelated containers' fast restart capability.
claims.acceptance_test: Update cleanup preview identifies exact host images to be removed and leaves unrelated-service images unless operator explicitly selects them.

claims.capability: A store administrator can attach an internal Lightning node or configure a custom external node and test the connection.
claims.merchant_outcome: Store can use a configured node once the node is enabled and connected/online.
claims.trigger: Store > Lightning choose internal or custom node and save/test
claims.behavior: Internal node selection saves and should show Public Node Info Online; external config can be tested before save; node won't accept LN payments until online.
preconditions: Bitcoin on-chain node fully synchronized for internal node
Lightning implementation enabled; credentials/endpoints valid
qualifiers: Documented built-in implementations include LND, CLN and Eclair; external connection modes vary
recovery_edge_cases: Check node enabled/sync, restart or troubleshoot connection if offline
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Show per-store payment readiness with node online and chain sync checks before enabling Lightning checkout.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Can accept Lightning directly through a merchant-controlled node while retaining self-hosted operating options.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Node uptime and on-chain sync become merchant responsibilities; online status does not guarantee inbound liquidity or route success.
claims.acceptance_test: Connection test reports implementation and sync status; checkout enables LN only when node reports online and inbound capacity can settle a test payment.

claims.capability: Merchant must maintain suitable Lightning channel liquidity; inbound capacity can be acquired from peers/LSPs or through channel management, and balance needs ongoing adjustment.
claims.merchant_outcome: Merchant can plan for receiving and sending capacity and identify why an online node may not accept incoming payments.
claims.trigger: Prepare node to receive payments or rebalance operating liquidity
claims.behavior: Guide explains fund on-chain wallet, open channel, obtain inbound/outbound capacity, and continuously manage distribution; LSP offers paid services.
preconditions: Lightning node operating and on-chain wallet funded
Channel partner and sufficient funds selected
qualifiers: Liquidity availability depends on channel counterparties and network conditions; no fixed availability guarantee
recovery_edge_cases: A node can be online yet lack inbound capacity to receive payments
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Expose inbound capacity status with low-liquidity alerts and link to self-managed or third-party acquisition choices.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Lightning can make Bitcoin payments fast and low cost, but merchant self-operation trades third-party custody for liquidity management work.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: LSP service can simplify access but brings fees and counterparty reliance; self-managed channels require capital, skill and monitoring.
claims.acceptance_test: Capacity monitor distinguishes online connectivity from usable inbound capacity and alerts before the merchant can no longer receive expected payment sizes.

claims.capability: Operator should record implementation-specific Lightning node recovery material before transacting; guide directs LND users to seed backup and CLN users to hsm_secret backup.
claims.merchant_outcome: Merchant can preserve required node recovery material separately from ordinary store/on-chain wallet backups.
claims.trigger: Before opening channels or accepting LN value
claims.behavior: Setup guide points to LND seed in Server Settings > Services and CLN hsm_secret location, and warns channel backup has limitations.
preconditions: Node implementation known and recovery material accessible
qualifiers: Exact location and channel-recovery process are implementation/version dependent
recovery_edge_cases: On-chain wallet seed alone is not sufficient to recover all channel state
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Create implementation-aware setup checks that verify protected copies of all required recovery items without uploading secrets.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Self-custody is preserved only if merchant can recover the LN node; documented backup discipline enables that goal.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Additional sensitive material increases secure-storage burden and wrong/stale backups do not guarantee funds recovery.
claims.acceptance_test: For each supported implementation, operator completes an isolated documented recovery drill with correct current material and no secret uploaded to BTCPay service.

claims.capability: A self-hosted server has one internal Lightning node; server admin can allow non-admin registrants to use it, making the host's node operator responsible for shared-node policy and custody risk.
claims.merchant_outcome: Operator can make internal Lightning access available to stores on instance, with clear understanding of shared infrastructure and fund ownership implications.
claims.trigger: Enable policy allowing non-admin users to use internal node
claims.behavior: FAQ describes one internal node per self-hosted server and policy-gated registrant use; third-party hosting may place registrants' funds in host's wallet.
preconditions: Internal Lightning node available and admin enables policy
qualifiers: Do not infer all instances share one node or one custody model; policy and hosting configuration vary
recovery_edge_cases: Store's Lightning key/control may not be equivalent to its on-chain wallet setup; verify owner and withdrawal route
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Clearly label who controls node keys and where funds accrue before allowing shared internal-node use.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Shared infrastructure lowers operator setup burden but may route merchants into custodial arrangements that weaken self-custody.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: An easier onboarding route can be valuable for small merchants, while host control and counterparty risk must be explicit and independently recoverable.
claims.acceptance_test: Before enabling, merchant sees node owner, key controller, funds destination and withdrawal/recovery path and verifies a small test receipt/withdrawal.

claims.capability: Documentation describes BTCPay as a web app usable on devices with a web browser, while native BTCPay wallet app status is unresolved from the dated FAQ note.
claims.merchant_outcome: Merchant can access the web interface through a mobile browser, but these docs do not establish native BTCPay wallet availability as of the research date.
claims.trigger: Open BTCPay interface on mobile device
claims.behavior: FAQ says BTCPay Server is a web app rather than a mobile app and references a mobile app under development in 2023; it mentions separate LN and Bitcoin node mobile clients.
preconditions: Instance reachable and browser-compatible device
qualifiers: Native mobile app current status not verified; do not claim a mobile app is absent based solely on stale roadmap text
recovery_edge_cases: Mobile access depends on network and server availability; offline operation is not documented here
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Publish current mobile support matrix and label browser-based versus native app functions.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Mobile access modality is independent of Bitcoin's settlement properties.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Browser access can support mobility without app distribution, but does not provide offline payment acceptance or native wallet signing by itself.
claims.acceptance_test: Current official support page verifies supported mobile browser tasks and native app release status, including a mobile transaction and admin path.

claims.capability: BTCPay multisig setup guide currently requires invited participants to be Store Owners to assemble signer public keys.
claims.merchant_outcome: A merchant can configure shared multisig wallet setup, but participants receive broad store owner role under the documented workflow.
claims.trigger: Invite participants for multisig store setup
claims.behavior: Guide states participants must be invited as Store Owners and notes plans for narrower roles to reduce trust required.
preconditions: Participants create/derive public key data and accept invitation
qualifiers: Guide describes current limitation at inspection time; role architecture may change
recovery_edge_cases: Owner role increases access beyond providing a signing key; only invite trusted participants
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Allow a key-contributor role limited to wallet setup and signing workflow without full store configuration privileges.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: On-chain multisig can distribute spend authorization, yet requiring full store ownership expands trust to unrelated merchant data and settings.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Narrow roles reduce collaboration risk but add permission modeling and recovery complexity; 2-of-N thresholds also trade convenience against quorum resilience.
claims.acceptance_test: A participant can contribute xpub and sign required PSBT while being unable to modify payment settings, view unrelated customer records, or alter other store controls.

claims.capability: A merchant using a third-party BTCPay host cannot establish from the product documentation that host code is honest; documentation recommends public-key-only wallet setup and warns of future receive-address substitution risk.
claims.merchant_outcome: Merchant can reduce key disclosure to host and monitor independent wallet activity, while recognizing host can affect future payment destinations.
claims.trigger: Configure an externally operated BTCPay host
claims.behavior: Docs recommend avoiding hot wallet/high-value use, importing extended public key, independently monitoring wallet and not providing private key to host.
preconditions: Merchant evaluates host and can independently derive/check addresses
qualifiers: This is a trust warning, not a claim about any particular host
recovery_edge_cases: If displayed receiving address diverges from independent wallet derivation, halt new payments and investigate
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Offer a merchant-verifiable receive-address fingerprint and host trust disclosure before acceptance.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Public-key integration can preserve merchant signing control but self-hosting or independent verification is still needed to resist host substitution.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Third-party hosting reduces infrastructure burden but introduces availability, integrity and privacy reliance; self-hosting transfers operations to merchant.
claims.acceptance_test: Merchant verifies generated addresses against independent wallet; deliberate mismatch produces a clear stop-payment warning.

claims.capability: Greenfield API permissions can be restricted to one store by appending that store ID, and API keys cannot grant permissions the creating user does not hold.
claims.merchant_outcome: An integration can be constrained to a selected store and to the authority of its merchant user.
claims.trigger: Create key or approve interactive authorization
claims.behavior: Permission strings may be scoped with store identifier; requested permissions are intersected with user's authority; omitted permission list can result in unrestricted key.
preconditions: Permission exists on target instance and user has it
qualifiers: Endpoint-specific permission should be checked in the target instance /docs; permission inheritance may apply
recovery_edge_cases: Do not treat empty permission array as deny-all; review and reject unintended broad scope
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Default app authorization to selected store(s) and explicitly deny an empty or unrestricted permission request unless user opts in.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Narrow scopes can limit third-party operations around Bitcoin invoices and wallet permissions without changing merchant key ownership.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Some integrations need multiple permissions/stores; scope errors can break operations and must be visible before approval.
claims.acceptance_test: Key scoped to Store A succeeds for A, fails on Store B, and lacks any permission absent from creating user's authority.

claims.capability: A user can revoke its current or identified API key so that it can no longer be used; an authorized administrator may revoke a target user's key.
claims.merchant_outcome: Merchant can terminate a connected integration credential after exposure or when access is no longer needed.
claims.actor: key owner or authorized server administrator
claims.trigger: Use account API key screen or key revocation endpoint
claims.behavior: Greenfield API describes deleting current key, identified user key, or a target user's key; successful response means key is no longer usable.
preconditions: User has key access or server admin permission for another user's key
qualifiers: Revoking key interrupts integrations using it; rotate/reconnect required
recovery_edge_cases: Identify affected application and replace credential only after removing the compromised key
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Provide per-key last-used details and a guided revoke-and-reconnect path for connected apps.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Fast revocation limits a compromised credential's ability to mutate Bitcoin store settings or operate supported wallet endpoints.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Revocation can interrupt order payment tracking or operations until replacement key is approved.
claims.acceptance_test: After revoke, old key receives unauthorized response; newly authorized least-privilege key restores only expected operations.

claims.capability: BTCPay invoice webhooks distinguish payment seen in mempool, full invoice processing, blockchain confirmation/settlement, expiration and invalid payment events.
claims.merchant_outcome: A commerce backend can map invoice events to pending, settled, expired or invalid order states without treating any observed transaction as final settlement.
claims.trigger: Receive an invoice event
claims.behavior: Guide defines InvoiceReceivedPayment as mempool payment seen, InvoiceProcessing as full amount seen but unconfirmed, InvoicePaymentSettled as confirmed payment, InvoiceSettled as settlement conditions met, and InvoiceExpired/Invalid separately.
preconditions: Webhook signature validated and event mapped to invoice ID
qualifiers: Merchant fulfillment policy must determine whether confirmations required
recovery_edge_cases: Late, partial and overpaid payments may produce events after expiration; do not assume monotonic simplistic state
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Provide an integration event simulator and state transition examples covering late, partial, overpaid and confirmed cases.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: State distinctions matter for Bitcoin mempool/confirmation settlement and prevent mistaken fulfillment based only on zero-confirmation observation.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Waiting for confirmations can slow fulfillment; accepting unconfirmed payments adds double-spend/reorg exposure.
claims.acceptance_test: For generated mempool, confirmed, expired, late, partial and invalid scenarios, backend maps status according to configured confirmation policy.

claims.capability: Integration should reconcile an invoice using both base status and additionalStatus and can use GET when webhook events may be missed or ambiguous.
claims.merchant_outcome: Merchant backend can distinguish expired-but-paid-late, paid-partial, paid-over and other combined invoice outcomes.
claims.trigger: Process webhook sequence or reconciliation request
claims.behavior: Guide lists base states New/Processing/Settled/Expired/Invalid and additional states Invalid/Marked/None/PaidLate/PaidOver/PaidPartial; recommends checking both and fetching current invoice when needed.
preconditions: Backend has authorized invoice read permission and stored invoice ID
qualifiers: A current API read reflects available server state at query time, not independent proof outside the instance
recovery_edge_cases: Missed callbacks, duplicate events and delayed payments require safe idempotent reconciliation
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Expose a canonical state mapping helper with explicit handling for combined status and additionalStatus values.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Captures Bitcoin payment edge cases such as confirmation-after-expiry and partial/overpayment without a processor being final arbiter.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Additional state complexity raises integration engineering cost; neither webhook nor API status substitutes for business risk policy.
claims.acceptance_test: Backend reconciliation of each documented status/additionalStatus combination produces deterministic order state and does not fulfill a partial/invalid invoice.

claims.capability: The documented BTCPay PSBT send flow allows the user to change fee rate and optionally enable RBF fee increase.
claims.merchant_outcome: Wallet operator can choose a fee target and allow fee bumping if an initial transaction is underpriced.
claims.trigger: Create on-chain send transaction and open advanced options
claims.behavior: PSBT guide describes editing fee rate and setting Allow fee increase (RBF) to Yes; higher or lower user choice affects confirmation speed and replacement ability.
preconditions: Wallet has spendable inputs and signer supports transaction options
qualifiers: RBF setting optional; transaction fee/confirmation outcomes depend on network conditions
recovery_edge_cases: Too-low fee may delay confirmation; the guide describes RBF as a way to bump fee
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Show fee estimate confidence, current network context and explicit replacement consequences before signing.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Direct Bitcoin wallet send exposes fee and replaceability controls to the merchant rather than hiding them behind processor settlement.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Higher fee buys likely speed but can cost more; RBF can change transaction inputs/outputs and requires careful payee/business handling.
claims.acceptance_test: Operator chooses fee and RBF, signer displays matching fee/transaction properties, and a test replacement is traceable as same spend intent.

claims.capability: BTCPay's documented PSBT flow exports a partially signed transaction for external signing and reimports the signed PSBT; the guide notes a non-witness UTXO option needed by some hardware signers.
claims.merchant_outcome: An offline signer or separate employee can inspect and sign a spend without signing key residing in BTCPay host.
claims.trigger: Choose PSBT signing and export transaction file
claims.behavior: User downloads PSBT, external wallet signs it, then signed file is imported; guide recommends Always include non-witness UTXO if available for BitBox02 example compatibility.
preconditions: Compatible signer and correct wallet metadata; destination/amount/fee reviewed
qualifiers: Example device-specific setting may not apply to every signer
recovery_edge_cases: If signer rejects file, verify supported PSBT version and required UTXO data; do not bypass transaction review
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Detect signer capability and select interoperable PSBT data automatically while showing the exact transaction to verify.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: PSBT provides an interoperable path to self-custodial hardware and air-gapped signing.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: File transfer and metadata compatibility add operator steps; more included data may disclose transaction history to signer.
claims.acceptance_test: Two supported signer types round-trip PSBT; signed transaction outputs and fee match the BTCPay transaction preview exactly.

claims.capability: Server administrators can browse the plugin directory and see a plugin's description, author, supported BTCPay versions, source link and user reviews; a listing does not mean it is installed.
claims.merchant_outcome: Operator can discover extension options and review compatibility/provenance before installing, while store users can distinguish missing feature from uninstalled plugin.
claims.trigger: Open Plugin Directory or Installed Plugins
claims.behavior: Directory lists discoverable plugin records; installed features appear only after admin installation and may be store-specific.
preconditions: Instance exposes plugin management and directory access
qualifiers: Directory metadata/reviews are not an audit or endorsement
recovery_edge_cases: Store user should ask admin to install missing plugin and consult plugin's own setup instructions
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Label directory entries clearly as available, installed, enabled, compatible, and configured per store.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Plugin discoverability is general extensibility; plugin content may or may not relate to Bitcoin.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Directory convenience can encourage trust by presence; version/source review remains required.
claims.acceptance_test: Directory listing is never shown as active feature until compatible plugin installation and store configuration are verified.

claims.capability: Only server administrators can install or remove a plugin; installation/removal is scheduled and applied at a server restart.
claims.merchant_outcome: Instance operator controls extension lifecycle and can verify installed state after restart.
claims.trigger: Select a plugin version and confirm install, or uninstall installed plugin
claims.behavior: BTCPay queues the change, prompts restart, is temporarily unavailable while restarting, and lets admin verify afterward under Installed Plugins.
preconditions: Admin role, selected plugin version and restart access
qualifiers: Plugin-specific configuration may still be required after installation; stores may rely on plugin before removal
recovery_edge_cases: Check store dependencies before uninstall; if restart fails plugin state may need operator recovery
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Show affected stores and plugin-dependent features before removal and provide a restart health check.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Lifecycle applies to all extensions; an installed plugin could alter payment behavior but this generic mechanism does not itself favor Bitcoin.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Central admin control can protect merchant environment but creates admin bottleneck and restart downtime.
claims.acceptance_test: Non-admin install/removal is denied; admin change remains queued until restart, then appears in correct installed/uninstalled state.

claims.capability: Docker recovery requires both saved data archives and a prepared compatible deployment profile; generated Compose file is disposable, while volumes, databases and generated secrets are persistent state.
claims.merchant_outcome: Operator can prepare a destination using deployment settings and restore persistent state without assuming generated configuration alone is a complete backup.
claims.trigger: Plan recovery or move instance to another host
claims.behavior: Architecture and restore docs distinguish generated Compose from persistent data and require compatible checkout, saved environment profile, generated Compose and BTCPay volume before restore.
preconditions: Operator preserved environment/deployment options and matching network/chains/plugins configuration
qualifiers: Docker-specific and setup dependent; blockchain data is re-synchronized rather than included
recovery_edge_cases: Missing secrets/profile or mismatched chain/Lightning configuration can prevent recovery or cause incorrect operation
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Generate an exportable deployment manifest alongside backup and run destination compatibility preflight.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Merchant can reconstruct its own processor and node deployment from retained state rather than depend on a platform-hosted processor.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Self-hosting means merchant must preserve configuration, secrets and version compatibility; large blockchain must resync and delays readiness.
claims.acceptance_test: Backup plus retained manifest rebuilds compatible isolated deployment, restores data and verifies chain sync without manual reconstruction of undocumented parameters.

claims.capability: BTCPay's Docker backup guide says Core Lightning's existing backup behavior is unchanged and its LND SCB recovery procedure does not apply to CLN; the inspected official pages do not specify an equivalent end-to-end CLN or Eclair restore procedure.
claims.merchant_outcome: Operator must use implementation-specific channel recovery guidance and cannot assume LND seed/SCB steps recover another implementation.
claims.trigger: Plan default backup, disaster recovery or migration for CLN/Eclair
claims.behavior: Docs explicitly limit SCB steps to Bitcoin LND and direct other implementations to their migration/static-channel backup guidance; CLN setup identifies hsm_secret as recovery material but does not make that alone a full channel-state recovery plan.
preconditions: Operator identifies Lightning implementation and consults its current official recovery documentation
qualifiers: Unknown details are left unknown; no inference that CLN/Eclair recovery is impossible or unsupported
recovery_edge_cases: Do not apply LND channel.backup import commands to CLN/Eclair; preserve source state and seek implementation-specific procedure
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Publish and link a BTCPay per-implementation backup/restore decision tree with tested, version-qualified steps.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Self-hosted LN implementation choice supports merchant autonomy but recovery documentation fragmentation increases risk across node implementations.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: A common BTCPay archive can simplify some data recovery, yet implementation-specific channel-state rules cannot be flattened safely into one generic restore recipe.
claims.acceptance_test: For every supported LN implementation, isolated backup and restore drills establish state preservation or documented recovery path without starting stale channel state against peers.

claims.capability: BTCPay internal wallet randomly enables or disables RBF by default across transactions, according to its Wallet FAQ.
claims.merchant_outcome: Merchant cannot assume every outgoing wallet transaction will signal replaceability unless it inspects transaction details/settings.
claims.trigger: Create an on-chain spend using internal wallet
claims.behavior: FAQ says RBF capability is randomly enabled/disabled between transactions for enhanced privacy; a separate PSBT guide shows optional fee increase setting in that workflow.
preconditions: Use BTCPay internal wallet; exact behavior may depend on transaction flow/version
qualifiers: FAQ does not document randomization algorithm or per-version behavior
recovery_edge_cases: If transaction fee proves insufficient, fee bump may not be available on a non-RBF transaction
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Expose replaceability state clearly before signing and offer intentional, privacy-aware selection where supported.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Randomized RBF is documented as a privacy measure, while predictable fee bumping can aid merchant transaction management.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: RBF improves fee recovery when signaled but can complicate zero-confirmation acceptance and transaction monitoring; randomized policy limits user predictability.
claims.acceptance_test: Before signing, user can determine whether a specific transaction is replaceable; test fee-bump action is offered only when supported and updates transaction lineage.

claims.capability: BTCPay Docker setup enables Bitcoin Core mempoolfullrbf policy by default, with a documented opt-out fragment.
claims.merchant_outcome: Operator can configure node mempool replacement policy that affects how conflicting unconfirmed payments are handled and observed.
claims.trigger: Configure setup fragments and rerun setup
claims.behavior: Wallet FAQ says mempoolfullrbf=1 is default in BTCPay setup and describes opt-mempoolfullrbf exclusion for operators who opt out.
preconditions: Docker deployment uses default fragment unless excluded
qualifiers: Mempool policy is node-local policy and not consensus rule; tradeoffs are explicitly contested in docs
recovery_edge_cases: Without full-RBF policy, FAQ notes merchant may learn about a non-RBF double spend only after confirmation; enabling policy can make zero-confirmation acceptance harder as policy spreads
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Present policy choice with explicit merchant detection benefit and network/zero-confirmation tradeoff, retaining operator choice.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Merchant conflict detection incentives and network propagation policy interests can diverge; classify as a tradeoff rather than assume the merchant-facing default is universally Bitcoin-positive.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Improved conflict visibility for the merchant may reduce zero-confirmation acceptance availability and affects node policy externalities; opt-out preserves operator control.
claims.acceptance_test: Operator can confirm configured node mempool policy and opt out; integration tests show expected replacement observation while no flow represents unconfirmed payment as settled.

claims.capability: BTCPay Server 1.0.4.0 historical release documentation described Advanced Settings coin selection for a spend, with wallet labels available to help organize desirable coins.
claims.merchant_outcome: At the documented 2020 release, wallet operator could choose specific coins for a transaction and use labels to aid UTXO management.
claims.trigger: Create transaction in the then-documented internal wallet and open Advanced Settings
claims.behavior: The release announcement says coin selection let users craft transactions using coins desirable for that payment situation and worked with wallet labels.
preconditions: BTCPay Server 1.0.4.0-era wallet behavior as described in release post
qualifiers: Historical version-specific source only; present-day UI, supported wallet modes, and current selection policy remain unresolved
Privacy framing in the source is not proof of CoinJoin, anonymity, or improved privacy for any particular spend
recovery_edge_cases: Do not assume user-selected inputs persist across upgrade or are supported in every current transaction workflow
claims.improvement_hypothesis: Document current supported coin-selection behavior and version coverage, including clear UTXO selection and change/fee review if still available.
claims.bitcoin_hypothesis: Explicit input selection can help operators manage UTXOs and spending intent, but any privacy benefit depends on transaction composition and external observers; avoid promising privacy outcomes.
claims.bitcoin_tradeoffs: Manual selection increases control but raises complexity and can create unintended linkage or uneconomic outputs if used without expertise.
claims.acceptance_test: For the current supported version, confirm which wallet modes expose input selection and that selected inputs, change, destination and fee match the signed transaction; separately assess privacy claims rather than infer them.

limitations: Research is based on official BTCPay Server documentation pages and documentation search extracts inspected on 2026-11-17. No software or integration was run, so these are documented behaviors, not compatibility test results.

Target instance version, plugins, hosting, deployment profile, authentication policies, wallet type, and Lightning implementation can change behavior. Use that instance's /docs and current operator configuration for implementation decisions.

Backup/restore operation details are specifically Docker deployment; detailed channel recovery claims are specific to Bitcoin LND with default bbolt backend. Other Lightning implementations remain unresolved here.
The mobile FAQ contains dated 2023 roadmap language; current native app status was not inferred from it.
This bundle excludes assigned merchant POS/invoice/payment-request/refund/payout UX and report claims, and does not claim all BTCPay features or all Bitcoin merchant jobs are covered.
